title: A Seat at the Table: Knowledge, Inheritance, and the Purpose of Schooling
author: David Didau
summary: Didau's case for the knowledge-rich curriculum rescues the term from caricature (rote memorization, silent classrooms, stripped agency) by reframing it around evidence from cognitive science: knowledge is the precondition for every higher-order skill schools claim to value; you cannot think well about what you know nothing about. Curriculum is not a neutral technical exercise but a promise made to young people about what they will need to understand the world they are entering. Subjects are distinct intellectual traditions with their own criteria for explanation and evidence, and pupils are apprenticed into them through carefully chosen scholarly tasks. The democratic payoff is sharp: public discourse assumes historical, scientific, and literary reference; if only the already advantaged can follow it, schools have failed their civic function. The remaining gap is writing instruction, where knowledge-rich intent too often meets skills-poor enactment.
points: Knowledge is not a neutral technical exercise but a promise to young people about what they will need to understand the world they are entering.
The core claim from cognitive science is direct: knowledge is the precondition for every higher-order skill schools say they value.
Subjects are distinct intellectual traditions with their own criteria for explanation, argument, and evidence; pupils are apprenticed through scholarly tasks, not generic engagement activities.
The democratic function of a knowledge-rich curriculum is to make public discourse (which assumes historical, scientific, and literary reference) intelligible to all, not just the already advantaged.
Knowledge-rich intent too often meets skills-poor enactment; the teaching of how sentences do intellectual work must be as rigorous as the selection of content itself.
quotes: For some, it has somehow come to mean rote memorisation, silent classrooms and pupils treated as passive containers for information. For others, it signals centralised curriculum packages, compliance masquerading as rigour and the belief that learning is distilled to the delivery and testing of facts, facts and more facts.
At its core, a knowledge-rich curriculum is not a claim about how much pupils know, but about what knowledge does. It begins from a view of thinking as something that depends on what is known.
Without it, analysis becomes opinion dressed as insight, creativity collapses into improvisation without constraint, and critical thinking degenerates into reflexive conspiracy theory generation.

As Christine Counsell has argued, curriculum is a promise made to future teachers. It is a commitment about what we believe young people will need in order to understand the world they are entering, not just cope with the next assessment.

There have been “lethal mutations”, cases where poor implementation reduced curriculum to rote learning and stripped teachers of agency, turning curriculum into something “done to” them rather than “done with” them.
The collection insists that subjects are not interchangeable delivery systems but distinct intellectual traditions, each with its own criteria for explanation, argument and evidence.
As Dylan Wiliam argues, “If exams were abolished tomorrow, advocates would still believe in a knowledge-rich approach as the right thing to do”. The reason is democratic.

Knowledge-rich intent too often meets skills-poor enactment. The result is frustration mistaken for high standards. If knowledge is to be genuinely empowering, the means of expressing it must be taught with the same care as the content itself.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
